Larry Ellison has cancelled a trading plan that would have let him sell up to 50 million Oracle shares by 24 October, a day after the plan was disclosed and with no stock sold under it. The instrument is a Rule 10b5-1 plan, an American safe harbour with no European counterpart, because EU market abuse rules bar managers from dealing in the 30 calendar days before results instead. Larry Ellison has cancelled the plan that would have let him sell up to 50 million Oracle shares, a day after it was disclosed, Bloomberg reported. “No Oracle stock was sold under that plan, and he has no other plans to sell any of his Oracle stock,” the company said. The plan was adopted on 22 June and would have run to 24 October. The shares were worth about $8.75B then and about $7.5B now, after a 16% fall. Oracle described it as a 10b5-1 plan in its statement. Ellison controls about 40% of the company and is its executive chair and chief technology officer. The timing was the problem. Oracle reported shrinking gross margins on Thursday, its shares fell 1.7% on Friday, and the same week it raised the cost of its job cuts to $2.8B. A Rule 10b5-1 plan is a piece of American market plumbing with no European equivalent. An executive who adopts one while not holding inside information can let trades execute later on a fixed schedule, including in periods when selling at their own discretion would draw questions. The rule dates from 2000, and the SEC tightened what has to be disclosed about these plans in 2022. Europe closes the window instead. Under the Market Abuse Regulation, a person discharging managerial responsibilities may not deal in the company’s shares during the 30 calendar days before an interim or year-end report. There is no adopt-in-advance exemption from that. Europe also discloses different things. It publishes transactions rather than intentions, within three working days of each deal, once EUR 5,000 has been reached in a calendar year. A plan that never traded would have left no trace at all. None of which suggests Ellison did anything improper. No shares were sold, and the plan was disclosed exactly as American rules require, which is the only reason anybody knew about it. But the two regimes would have produced different weeks. Europe would never have published a plan for the market to read, and would not have let one run through the results of a company sitting one notch above junk. The K-shaped economy and the AI bubble are sowing the seeds of the next crash. That's the message from Henrik Zeberg, a Danish economist who sees a roller coaster ride ahead for the US economy and stock market. In his view, equities are headed for a massive "blow-off top" sometime before the end of the year, with stocks tumbling from their peaks the economy entering a recession. If thing play out the way his models are forecasting, it could involve the Nasdaq 100 soaring as high as 39,000 by late 2026 — an increase of around 32% — before plummeting back to around 10,600, its 2022 trough, he told Business Insider in a recent interview. A decline of that magnitude would mark a 72% crash from the peak Zeberg predicts, and would be on par with the dot-com crash that saw the Nasdaq 100 plunge 83% from its 2000 peak to the low in 2002. "I think we will see a 2000-scenario," the macro strategist at the investment firm Swissblock said, speculating that a sharp drop in markets could later be followed by broader distress in the financial system, such as in banking and private credit. "I think that run is going to be quite devastating," he added of the AI bubble bursting. Zeberg, who's studied business cycles for 20 years, said he drew much of his thesis from an economic model he created, which analyzes the state of the economy and finds parallels with past cycles. The model — which correctly predicted the 2020 downturn and dismissed a recession when investors were worried about one in 2022 — now shows the US is heading into an economic contraction, Zeberg said. That's at odds with what recent economic data is showing on the surface. Hiring in the US blew past expectations in August, with the US adding 162,000 jobs, nearly triple economists' estimates. GDP growth, meanwhile, is expected to accelerate to 4.7% in the third quarter, more than triple its pace in the second quarter, according to the latest estimate from the Atlanta Fed. But those positive data points are largely a distortion stemming from the growing gap between top earnings and lower- to middle-income households, Zeberg said, pointing to signs that the real economy is struggling under the surface: Job growth crushed expectations last month, but the labor force participation rate has generally declined in recent years, falling to a 50-year low in July. The long-term unemployment rate — the measure of workers who have been unemployed for at least 27 weeks — has also climbed higher, clocking in at 27% in August, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Most of the job gains for the past year may be revised away, Zeberg speculated. Last year, numbers were revised to show the US added 911,000 fewer jobs from April 2024 to March 2025 than initially reported. Housing, considered to be a major engine of the economy, has been sluggish in the years since the pandemic, with higher mortgage rates, stubbornly high prices, and general economic uncertainty curtailing transaction activity. Existing home sales fell 2% in August, according to data from the National Association of Realtors, even as a 10-year record of homes for sale sits idle on the market. "Housing is the most rate-sensitive sector in the economy. It is a financed asset. When money gets expensive, housing feels it first," Zeberg wrote in a post explaining his thesis on Substack. Zeberg said more lower- and middle-income Americans were showing signs of distress due to factors like higher inflation and rising borrowing costs. A second-quarter survey conducted by Primerica found that 7% of middle-class Americans said their income was falling behind the cost of living. 58% they wouldn't be able to cover an emergency expense of at least $1,000. The personal savings rate has also collapsed over the last five years, with Americans saving an average 3% of their disposable income in July, down from 9.5% in 2021, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. Most growth in the US is attributed to the tech sector and the cohort of top earners, Zeberg said. Fixed investment in the IT sector alone accounted for 5% of GDP in the second quarter, per an estimate from Fitch Ratings. "It's not a real boom," he said of the strength of the US economy. "Normally, corporate profits can keep going up even into the recession, but the moment the story breaks for the consumer, that's the moment it's breaking for the businesses as well." Zeberg said the issues facing the broader economy would catch up to financial markets in four stages. Here's how he thinks the coming year could play out: Timing: Present to late 2026 What happens: The US economy continues to weaken, but any hint of bad economic news causes investors to price in rate cuts, which sparks a "vertical" rally in stocks, Zeberg predicts. Other assets, like crypto and gold, would also soar, while the US dollar falls in value as investors price in lower rates, he added. In the final stages of the rally, Zeberg thinks the Nasdaq 100 could climb to 37,000 to 39,000. The market is currently more focused on rate hikes instead of cuts. Investors are pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points at its policy meeting next week, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Timing: Q4 of 2026 What happens: The economy will likely roll over "for real" in October or November, due to weakness in the labor market and other areas. That causes the Fed to step in and cut interest rates, leading the US dollar to fall further in value, Zeberg said. The US Dollar Index, which measures the value of the greenback against a basket of foreign currencies, could fall to a level of around 93 to 94, Zeberg predicts. Once the US dollar hits that level, stocks will likely hit a peak, he added, citing his technical analysis framework. Equities could then see a "violent" drop over the course of three to four weeks, Zeberg said. He speculated that the drop will likely be triggered by a single event, such as a tech giant missing on earnings. Timing: Q1 to Q2 of 2027 What happens: US stocks resume their path higher temporarily as investors attempt to recover from the year-end sell-off. At the same time, the US economy will enter a recession "invisibly," Zeberg said. After a brief rally, Zeberg expects stocks to resume their decline and Treasury yields to drop rapidly as markets price in economic weakness and support from the Fed. Meanwhile, distress could begin to surface in other areas of the economy, Zeberg said, pointing to the possibility of more loans being marked down in the private credit sector while funds continue to halt redemptions. Timing: Q2 to Q3 of 2027 What happens: Markets could see a final reckoning in the form of a Black Swan event, Zeberg said, pointing to structural problems like high leverage in financial markets and the circular nature of many AI deals as potential sources. At that point, stocks will tumble back to 2022 lows, while the US dollar soars as investors around the world scramble to store their wealth in dollar-denominated safe havens. Zeberg said he would be watching for two signals to tell when investors should head for the hills: Zeberg said he'd revisit this thesis if yields were to stabilize around their current levels, or if activity in the housing or job market picked up meaningfully in the coming months. Zeberg's thesis lies on the fringes of Wall Street, where most forecasters are expecting the AI boom to last for at least several more years. Still, more investors are turning a cautious eye toward the strength of the US economy, with concerns swirling around inflation as oil tops $100 a barrel again. The EU's seven gigafactories are due to run by mid-2028, which works only if nothing else slips, and about EUR 1bn of the EUR 30bn is actually committed Artificial Intelligence Chip China’s AI industry is moving from competing on models to deploying agents, and the China Telecom Research Institute expects inference to reach 80% of the country’s compute market by 2029. Europe’s answer is seven gigafactories whose bids close in November and whose machines are due to run by mid-2028, on a EUR 30bn budget of which around EUR 1bn is secured. China’s AI industry is shifting from competing on large models and raw computing power towards deploying and selling AI agents, a report says. It expects agents to drive close to tenfold annual growth in the country’s computing demand over the next two to three years. The report comes from the China Telecom Research Institute, the research arm of the state-owned carrier, and was carried by the state broadcaster CCTV on Saturday. Its sharpest figure is a split. Inference will account for 80% of China’s computing-power market by 2029, overtaking demand from training. Training builds a model once. Inference is what it costs every time somebody uses one, which makes it an operating expense rather than a capital one. Chinese technology companies are expected to spend close to 600 billion yuan, about $89B, on AI this year. The report puts that at more than a tenth of all investment in the country. Europe is building for the same demand on a different clock. The Commission opened bidding in July for up to seven gigafactories, a EUR 30B programme with about EUR 10B of public money and EUR 20B hoped for from private investors. Roughly EUR 1B of it is actually committed. Chinese technology companies are on course to spend that much on AI about every five days this year. Applications close on 12 November, awards are expected in early 2027, construction starts that year, and the machines are due to run by mid-2028. On paper that arrives a year before China’s crossover. It assumes nothing else slips. Things have slipped. Bidding moved from May to July, the evaluation criteria were delayed more than once, and interest fell from about 70 interested companies to roughly ten expected bidders. The money is the larger question. Most of the public half depends on a budget for 2028 to 2035 that member states have not agreed. Meanwhile the economics have moved. Inference is where the margin sits, and the companies capturing it are optimising models rather than building them. China’s report is a forecast about running models, and Europe is still deciding where to put the buildings. Two thirds of Oracle's workforce sits outside the US, and in the EU a planned redundancy runs on a statutory clock that a court ruling last October made unforgiving Oracle’s offices in the Pipera business district of Bucharest, photographed at night. Oracle has raised the cost of its 2026 restructuring by $700M to about $2.8B, covering actions it says it expects to take, and disclosed a plan letting Larry Ellison sell 50 million shares by 24 October. Roughly 92,000 of its 141,000 staff work outside the US, and in the EU collective redundancies require consultation, written notice to the authorities and a 30-day standstill. Oracle has raised the cost of this year’s job cuts by $700M to about $2.8B, Bloomberg reported, most of it severance. It has already booked around $2.1B of that. The increase covers “additional actions that we expect to take“, the company said in a filing. Those cuts have not happened yet. Chief financial officer Hilary Maxson told analysts that “simplification and efficiency actions” were helping protect margins. Most of the people who could be affected are not American. Oracle had about 49,000 staff in the US at the end of May and roughly 92,000 elsewhere, after headcount fell about 13% in a year to 141,000. In the European Union, actions a company expects to take run on a statutory clock. The Collective Redundancies Directive covers cuts above set thresholds. It requires an employer planning them to consult workers’ representatives in good time and with a view to reaching an agreement, on how to avoid the redundancies or reduce the number affected. It must then notify the competent public authority in writing. The redundancies take effect no earlier than 30 days after that notification, and member states may extend the period to 60. Getting it wrong became more expensive last October, when the Court of Justice ruled that a failure to notify makes the dismissals invalid and that the defect cannot be cured afterwards. Romania shows the shape of it. Oracle employs about 4,000 people there and cut around 500 in June, after roughly 400 in late 2025. Both rounds came out of a plan set the previous financial year, and a former employee said at the time that more was expected. The money is going into data centres. Oracle is building capacity for customers including OpenAI, burned about $24B of cash after capital spending last year, and S&P has cut it to BBB-, one notch above junk. Larry Ellison, who owns about 40% of the stock, adopted a trading plan on 22 June that lets him sell 50 million shares through 24 October. At the closing price that day those shares were worth $8.75B. The stock has fallen 16% since, and the severance bill is $2.8B. The United States stock market crashed in 1929, and the Roaring â20s came tumbling down. Banks closed, incomes fell, and citizens across the country lost their jobs and homes. The Dust Bowl destroyed farmland as crop prices dropped, driving many farms into foreclosure. Families saw their life savings disappear and had to become resourceful, making do with very little.Â  According to Encyclopedia Britannica, Americans had plunged into "the worst depression ever experienced by a world economy," not knowing that their survival would one day be stamped in the history books. While the crash affected the entire United States, some states saw higher unemployment rates and income drops than others. Many relied on basic resources, government relief programs, and community support just to make it to the next day.Â  Here's why the Great Depression occurred and where America was hit hardest. Several factors fueled the economic collapse of the late 1920s and early 1930s. According to History, mass consumption after World War I left businesses "vulnerable to sudden shifts in consumer confidence." Countries that once worked together to run the international financial system before the war were now at odds. Questionable get-rich-quick schemes multiplied throughout the Roaring â20s. American investors bought stocks "on margin," borrowing up to 90% of the price from banks. When the market crashed in October 1929, investors raced to withdraw their money and sell their stocks, causing a ripple effect, according to American University economics professor Mary Eschelbach Hansen. "It had a wealth effect on consumption (when peopleâs wealth falls, they consume less), and it also made consumers and firms pessimistic. Then came a series of banking panics and failures. Households lost more of their wealth, and the lines of credit that firms used were disrupted. Unemployment soared." Created in 1913 to promote economic stability, the Federal Reserve System actually helped accelerate the Great Depression. Interest rates declined, citizens over invested, and the money supply (which grew 67% from 1921 to 1929) was contracted in an attempt to temper the stock market, until it slowed too drastically. Another factor in the Great Depression was the Gold Standard. When the stock market crashed, investors began trading their dollars for gold. The Fed responded to the dollarâs declining value by raising interest rates, which caused businesses to close and impacted the livelihoods of ordinary families across the nation. As if this werenât enough to topple the economy, President Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Act in 1930, raising U.S. tariffs. Other countries retaliated by slapping tariffs on U.S. exports, lowering demand for American products abroad. The U.S. economy did not return to normalcy until around 1940, amid the onset of another World War. Increased government spending, job creation, and President Franklin Delano Roosevelt signing the New Deal helped support recovery after the Great Depression. Not all states experienced the Great Depression in the same way. According to the National Bureau of Economic Research, income declined more in some regions than others; South Dakota experienced the greatest loss of work, while Maryland experienced the least. The states hit hardest by the Great Depression were those in the Dust Bowl: Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nebraska. These states simultaneously faced both a collapsing economy and a drought. As a result, by the end of the Great Depression, 200,000 Americans had left the Great Plains for California. States in the South Atlantic, like Maryland, were less affected than the Plains because they had more industries. Working in NYC real estate, brokering deals for the rich and famous in one of the most desirable property markets in the world, is a "glamorous" business. Yet, for broker Violetta Kruglyak, that does not translate to a glamorous life. For her, breaking into the real estate world is defined by one word: hustle. She might work for a firm that sells luxury Manhattan townhouses — but there is a lot of behind-the-scenes work, tight budgeting, and trial and error that go into being successful in the competitive and dynamic NYC real estate business. Kruglyak, 44, originally from Odessa, Ukraine, moved to NYC in 2011 after getting married, having taught herself English while growing up. Fifteen years later, she still thinks in Russian, raises her 17-year-old son as a single mother, owns her dream sports car, and has worked her way up to become a make-up and hair stylist and a broker at luxury residential and commercial brokerage firm Nest Seekers International. Kruglyak is one of the people Business Insider has interviewed for our Cost of the City series, where we dive into the lives of New Yorkers and the trade-offs they face to stay in one of the most expensive cities in the country. How has your experience living and affording New York City been? What challenges have you faced and how have you adapted? Talk to a reporter about your experience: reach out to mros@businessinsider.com or fill out this form so we can contact you. There have been times when Kruglyak has considered moving away from NYC, especially when she was struggling financially. In 2020, after losing her last full-time job as a beauty advisor at Nordstrom, she went into credit card debt to make ends meet. This is when she decided to pursue a career with a higher financial ceiling. After watching the first episode of "Owning Manhattan," a reality TV show that follows NYC celebrity real estate broker Ryan Serhant, she signed up for a course to get her broker's license and entered the industry in 2024. What surprised her was how long the process is: It can take two months to a year between the moment you begin a deal and finally closing it and getting a commission. This makes cash flow and income inconsistent for people in the real estate industry. "You have to run a lot to find the deal, to find those people, to find apartments," she said. "It's a lot of cold calls. It's a lot of rejection." While working in both beauty and real estate allows Kruglyak to tap into the luxurious NYC lifestyle, she does not necessarily live it. Everyone is dressed up. But it's so much to learn if you want to be a real professional and make people trust you and do deals," she said. "You have to completely forget all your ego and what you knew, and just be a student." Throughout her time in NYC, Kruglyak built a career in cosmetics and luxury retail, working for brands and stores including Chanel, Bloomingdale's, Bergdorf Goodman, and Nordstrom. Alongside her sales work, she studied English, trained as a makeup artist, and earned an NYC tour guide license. While being a stylist and a broker are different jobs, they feed off of one thing Kruglyak knows how to manage: people and connections. "Each of my jobs and experiences brought me to this. That's why I'm so comfortable in real estate — because it's still people," she said. "You really have to be creative, think on the go, and you cannot teach that by the book." Her network of clients as a makeup and hair stylist has grown over the last 10 years, where she charges $200 for a makeup look and around $1,000 per day to help out at a photo shoot. The weekly calls and referrals she gets for makeup jobs help sustain her as she continues her main focus on growing as a broker, and some of her beauty clients have become real estate clients. "One month it can be up to $10,000, and I'm like, OK, I'm rich. Another month, it can be like hardly $4000, which is nothing and very challenging," she said. "It's scary, but at the same time, so motivating." Managing a fluctuating income requires discipline. Kruglyak saves as much as possible from each paycheck and plans months in advance. "I'm growing, so I'm not as stable financially, but I already can see it's definitely better," she said. The market has changed due to new regulations around who pays for brokers in New York City. Since the FARE Act, which banned the formerly common practice of tenants being on the hook for broker fees, took effect in June 2025, Kruglyak said it has become easier for brokers to collect their fees directly from landlords. Still, she said she has seen more rental units, especially well-priced ones, come off the market. Rents have also risen sharply from a year earlier. "Last summer, I could find a studio for like $2,600, for example. Now it's impossible. The same studio is going to be like $3,500, for the same size, in Manhattan," she said. As a single mother with no extended family in the country, Kruglyak has had to get creative to make ends meet. For someone in her situation, she emphasized: "You don't have plan B — only success." She pays around $2,900 for a 2-bedroom apartment in Coney Island with an ocean view. She has converted it into a 3-bedroom apartment and sometimes rents out the extra room. She is still paying off the debt, but has it under control. Although she has considered moving to Manhattan, her affordable Brooklyn rent keeps her from moving elsewhere. She has invested in her dream sports car — a Mercedes — and pays around $600 a month for insurance and $750 a month for the car payment. She goes to the gym daily with her Equinox membership and pays for sensual bachata dance classes at least once a week using her $120 monthly membership. The biggest trade-off for Kruglyak is time. Focusing most of her time on her work and son, she said she feels like she doesn't have much of a personal or social life, and rarely travels. "I even lost a few friendships because I'm mostly focused on career building," she said. "If I got the choice to go to some event or someone's birthday, I probably choose to stay with my son or study something." Yet, the image of successful New Yorkers around her keeps her going. "I think some people just expect that something's supposed to happen, but the mindset should be you create something to happen," she said. "People just leave — they give up, it's tough, it's expensive, it's hard — but I'm proud that, more or less, I made it, and I feel comfortable, and my child feels comfortable. There is a crisis plaguing the technology industry, and it all has to do with artificial intelligence (AI) data centers needing vast amounts of RAM. With the buildings having hundreds of powerful computers powering popular AI tools like Claude, Copilot, and Gemini, each one needs high-powered RAM in order to process data. The demand for more RAM means other companies, such as tablet makers, must spend more to purchase RAM for their devices. However, one tablet maker seems to be weathering the storm: Lenovo. Globally, the tablet market has seen reduced sales throughout 2026. The real strain hit in the second quarter when shipments fell by 10% year over year to 36 million units, according to Omdia. The only company that managed to ship tablets and see annual growth was Lenovo — not even Apple or Samsung saw increases. With an increase of 27% year on year, Lenovo's sales were due to demand from users as well as a preplanned marketing strategy from the company to ship tablets ahead of anticipated increases in prices. Lenovo also saw an opportunity to take advantage of major retail discounts and shipped to meet those deadlines. Lenovo also seems to be on the cutting edge of understanding the market. The company has shown off some cool new Lenovo tech concepts as well that consumers may be interested in using around the house to help them work, play, or study. One factor in Lenovo's success is where the company makes its tablets and other devices. With increased tariffs from the U.S. in place in countries such as China, Lenovo has used production plants outside of China. This may be what is helping the company ship more tablets than its competitors. There are, however, other reasons as well, with one being that Lenovo's tablets are cheaper. Looking at perhaps one of the most well-known tablet makers around, Apple, each of its tablets is marketed at a much higher price than Lenovo's. The iPad Pro starts at $1,199, while the smallest and lower-powered model, the iPad Air, begins at $599. Samsung's most expensive sits around $1,200, with its lower range being closer to $299.99. Acer's highest-costing tablet is $599.99, and its lowest is $119.99. Lenovo's highest priced tablet is $999.99, with its lowest costing just $99.99. All prices may change, but that initially low price makes it difficult to compete with Lenovo. Lenovo also generally tends to offer a wider selection of tablets when compared to Samsung, Apple, and other brands. Apple's line of tablets includes the iPad Air, iPad Mini, iPad Pro, and iPad. Even when put up against Samsung, Lenovo's website says it has 15 tablets, while Samsung only shows it sells 11. Acer, on the other hand, has 20 tablets on its site — among the most from all brands — but they aren't all as powerful, nor are they all as affordably priced as Lenovo. Lenovo tablets tend to be priced at a lower rate than those from competitors such as Acer, Samsung, and Apple. All three companies make various series of tablets with premium, mid-range, and lower-powered options available. The Lenovo Tab Plus Gen 2 is a mid-ranged priced tablet at $289.99 that has a 12.1-inch display, 2560 x 1600 resolution, and a MediaTek Dimensity 7400 Processor all on Android 16. A comparable tablet from Acer is the Iconia Duo D12 at $349.99. It has a larger 12.2-inch display, but a lower 1600 x 2400 resolution, and a less powerful MediaTek Helio G99 processor. Samsung makes the Galaxy Tab A11+, which is a comparable tablet to that of the Lenovo Tab Plus Gen 2. It has a smaller screen at 11-inches, a lower 1920 x 1200 resolution, and a not-as-powerful MediaTek MT8775 processor, all for $299.99. It's a little more expensive than the Lenovo, as well, but for a few more bucks you get a larger screen and more processing power. It seems even with the tablet market having issues selling and shipping devices, Lenovo has managed to find a way to make a profit. If you want to buy a Lenovo tablet while it still remains more affordable than other brands, start looking at these specific models. You may even be able to find a compact tablet perfect for entertainment.

The US transportation secretary has told Ford to cut ties with CATL and Geely, objecting among other things to the joint venture the carmaker is building with Geely at its plant in Valencia. The European Parliament is tightening a law that would require exactly that arrangement, forcing Chinese investors in strategic sectors into EU joint ventures capped at 49% and obliging them to transfer technology. The US transportation secretary has told Ford to cut its Chinese ties, and America’s China policy looks less settled the closer you read it, InsideEVs argued. Sean Duffy wrote to chief executive Jim Farley on 8 September citing “profound concern“. Three things bother him. A CATL battery licence in Michigan, a delay in moving Lincoln production out of China, and a joint venture with Geely at Ford’s plant in Spain. “When a company intentionally chooses to deepen operational dependencies on strategic competitors, it fails to act as the reliable partner the American public and this DOT require,” the letter said. Ford called it “a wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines“. Duffy did not allege that the company had broken any law. The Spanish venture is the part worth reading twice here. Ford and Geely agreed in July to build four models together at Valencia from 2028, with Ford holding 66% and Geely 34%. Brussels is drafting a law that would make that shape compulsory. Under the Industrial Accelerator Act, MEPs want investors from countries holding 40% of a global market to come in through a joint venture with an EU entity, cap their stake at 49%, and transfer technology to Europeans. Ford and Geely already clear the first two. The rapporteurs, Christophe Grudler, Pierre Jouvet and Anna Cavazzini, would also require 60% EU workers, 1% of annual revenue reinvested in European research and 30% of inputs sourced in the bloc. They want the rules to bite from EUR 50M rather than the Commission’s EUR 100M. The reason is that Europe has been paying for these partnerships and getting little back. Transport and Environment found no technology transfer requirements in Chinese-European battery tie-ups, despite EUR 900M of state aid for plants in Hungary and Poland and about EUR 300M for a CATL venture with Stellantis in Spain. Washington’s answer to a Chinese partnership is to break it. Brussels wants to price it instead. Both are aimed at the same fact, which is that Chinese firms now lead on batteries. Only one of the two still assumes the knowledge can travel back the other way. The EU duty on Chinese electric cars covers range extenders as well as pure battery models, which puts both of Li Auto's product lines on the taxed side of the line A Li Auto publicity image of the Li 6, the first model the company plans to sell in Europe. Li Auto will show the Li 6 at next month’s Paris Motor Show and start selling in Europe in the fourth quarter, six years earlier than its founder said it would. It is bringing only its battery models, because the EU’s duty on Chinese electric cars explicitly covers extended-range vehicles, the type that make up its business at home. Li Auto will show the car it intends to sell in Europe at next month’s Paris Motor Show and start selling in the fourth quarter, the company said. It has not named a country, a price or a sales channel. The i6 crossover becomes the Li 6 abroad, and the company drops “Auto” from its own name. This is a reversal. Founder Li Xiang said in 2023 that Li Auto had no plans to go global before 2028. Paris is a crowded room. More than a dozen Chinese brands are exhibiting from 13 October, among them BYD, XPeng, Zeekr and Leapmotor. What Li Auto is leaving at home is more revealing than what it is bringing. Europe gets the battery cars. The extended-range models are going to the Middle East and Central Asia instead. Those extended-range cars are the company’s business at home. Charging coverage is the obvious explanation and it is not the only one. The EU duty on Chinese battery electric vehicles covers cars propelled solely by electric motors, and the Commission’s published scope includes range extenders. A range extender burns petrol to generate electricity. The wheels are still turned by a motor, so for customs purposes the car is a battery electric vehicle. A plug-in hybrid is different, because its engine can drive the wheels. That is the gap through which 28% of Europe’s market for plug-in hybrids went to Chinese brands in the first half of this year. Li Auto has no equivalent move available. Both of its product lines sit on the taxed side of that line. The rate is the other unknown. Li Auto was not among the sampled manufacturers, so it faces either 20.7% as a cooperating exporter or 35.3% as a non-cooperating one, on top of the standard 10%, within a range that runs to 45.3%. The i6 starts at about $36,000 in China, where it is sold against the Tesla Model Y. Add a European price structure and either of those rates, and it arrives in a showroom next to a BMW iX3. Li Auto said in May it was targeting the second half. It has now committed to a quarter, a show and a name, and has said nothing about the number that decides whether any of it works. It's time to add another word to the founder dictionary. The term "LARP" started as an acronym for live action role play. LARPers wore costumes and adopted characters, imagining a video game-like world in real life. Then the internet adopted it, making it a stand-in for terms like "poser" or "faker." Now, the term is all the rage in startup land. A LARPer is someone who's playing founder more than actually being one. They loudly flex their work and the circles they run in, rather than fighting for customers. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan fashioned it into a warning: "Be earnest, don't larp." Intercom cofounder Des Traynor warned about it in a September email to Business Insider: "Look, you get one shot at this life, don't waste it LARPing as a startup founder for followers." Indeed, the founder-influencer type is growing — and it's hard to distinguish earnest marketing from performative hype-cycling. Is that 996 post a real portrayal of your hustle, or is it merely grindslop? > grab 10 founders you know > book a mansion in bali with a home gym> hire a private chef > lock the fuck in > 10x your revenue in 30 days > larp pic.twitter.com/sY313TYcF5 Posting about 996 on LinkedIn — but having an ultra-high screen time spent on the X app — was on Christian Di Bratto's list of attributes of an LARPing founder. Others he listed were sleeping on the floor of a WeWork and quoting Paul Graham essays like scripture. Graham himself has commented on the rise of LARPers and how difficult it is to spot them. He responded to a comment accusing Y Combinator of being full of LARP. "YC is pretty good at filtering them out at this point, but it's inevitable that a few will slip in," Graham wrote. "Especially among the younger founders, where larping is often indistinguishable from inexperience." Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    Tan asked Sam Altman about the LARPing accusations at YC Startup School in July. (Rather than pronouncing the acronym, Tan spelled out the words — "live action role play" — over and over.) Altman was confused: "They say that about YC specifically?" he asked, before questioning, "What's the claimed larp?" Altman ended up pivoting to talk about "haters on Twitter." Cosplaying founder isn't exactly new in Silicon Valley. One might call Elizabeth Holmes the godmother of LARPers. What is new, then, is the power of social media marketing. "Too many 'founders' these days need to quit larping and just admit they're content creators," wrote product designer Alec Freese. Declan Craggs, the mayor of Diss, Norfolk, said Diss Town Council has tried using ultrasonic sound devices and employing a falconer's hawks to scare the pigeons away from Mere Street, but nothing has worked. While many locals agree with the council's actions, others feel the pigeons were being unfairly demonised. The council has asked businesses in the town's centre to consider putting spikes and other deterrents on their building's front ledges.  Pigeon droppings and feathers are making Mere Street look dirty, residents have said Craggs has urged people to stop feeding the pigeons, with signs put up across the town - yet, he said, it has not stopped the problem.  "Some people are of the opinion pigeons have as much of a right to be here as we do, which is why we haven't taken these steps [to cull them] and are looking at just trying to keep the area tidy on a day-to-day basis," Craggs said. Susan French said both Norwich and Diss need to find solutions to the pigeon mess When speak to people and businesses on Mere Street, there was agreement that pigeons were causing mess, but there were differing views on how to tackle the issue. It has been edited for length and clarity.People often assume that I quit my six-figure job in product design because of severe burnout or an existential crisis, but that wasn't the case. I moved from Korea to Toronto in 2020 as an in-house product designer for a tech company, often creating mobile apps and websites. The paycheck was great — I was making about $173,000 to do a job that allowed me to have a fairly healthy work-life balance. I wasn't working 80 hours per week. Most weeks, I clocked about 40 hours, working mostly 9 to 5. Since my income was more than enough to live on, I was also able to travel when I had time off, never needing to worry about money or budgets. While I wouldn't say I loved the work, I liked it. The job was about making logical decisions, and then convincing stakeholders of my decisions through storytelling. It was my dream job as an immigrant, and it was sustainable. I could have carried on working it, but I had also been doing content creation on the side and had just signed a book deal. There weren't enough hours in the day to do all three. It would have been like having three full-time jobs. Debating which one to let go of, I decided to quit the most stable of the three — product design. Writing a book was very important to me, and I knew content creation would support the promotion of the book. But I was hesitant to abandon my only employed source of work. The thought was really scary. I remember having so much anxiety in the weeks leading up to my resignation in June 2026. Was it a mistake to leave a consistent paycheck in the middle of economic uncertainty? Would I be able to re-enter the market should I change my mind? I made a deal with myself to try and quell the anxiety that this was a permanent decision. For one year, I'd work for myself — pursuing content creation and book writing — and then I'd decide if I wanted to go back to the corporate world. Sure, I might not be able to go back to the same company or make the same salary if I choose to return, but I have a résumé with lots of examples of my work should I decide to return to being a product designer. Since resigning, every morning, I cycle to a gym and work out, and then head to an office and write from noon until 5 p.m. I fit in content creation throughout the day. I'm hoping to take my writing on the road and travel this year too. Rushing less, I feel like I'm existing more in the world, noticing myself and the world around me, choosing what I want to fill my time with. I had saved money, had a supportive partner, and knew it was possible on a practical level to give up my salary. But it hasn't been easy financially. Content creation payments are inconsistent. In July, I only made $6 because there was a delay in the content creation payment system. I've had portions of my book advance, but the income from my self-employment fluctuates a lot. Some months, I earn zero dollars and other months, I earn even more than I used to in my 9 to 5. I've had to mentally adapt to inconsistent pay, and rather than viewing it as a threat, seeing it as the reality of self-employment. Another difficulty has been setting boundaries. I could work 24 hours a day as my own boss because there is always more I can do. When I was employed, I'd shut my computer at the end of the day and be done. But being self-employed, my mind is always ticking over about work. I've had to get strict with myself to ensure I do have breaks. Three months in, I'm nearly always confident that I made the right decision to take this year out, though I do sometimes get shaken for a short time when people online tell me I've made a huge error. If I hadn't taken this chance to pursue another dream of working for myself, I would have regretted it. But who knows what will come of it. Even if I do return to the corporate world, this year wouldn't have been a mistake. I would have had the experience of leaving something that felt nice and stable for the unknown. Hisayuki Idekoba hears regularly about how broken hiring can feel. As head of the job platform Indeed, job seekers tell him they have applied to roles only to get nothing back, while employers complain about unresponsive candidates and surging application volumes, thanks in part to AI bots that flood open roles with résumés. "It's a vicious cycle," Idekoba said. He wants to break that loop by making Indeed's matching tools feel more like help from a recruiter for people applying cold. That means guiding job seekers toward roles where they are more likely to gain traction, while helping employers focus on applicants who are serious and relevant. Idekoba said better matching could discourage fruitless applications. He gave the example of a restaurant worker applying for a $200,000 engineering job rather than pursuing a more appropriate restaurant-management position. Ultimately, Idekoba said, the goal is to make better matches on both sides of the process. "How can we make sure job seekers are a real person, and it's not an AI application, and they're serious, and they're qualified," he said. "And how can we have real employers who are really trying to fill positions?" Indeed is navigating some of the same tensions Idekoba described. In July, it began a limited US test of Apply For Me, a tool that could automatically submit applications for job seekers. About a month later, it paused the feature after receiving feedback, saying it would instead focus on having users review drafted applications before hitting "submit." Questions about AI's role in the job search are unfolding in a labor market where few people are changing jobs. Overall job postings on Indeed were 1.8% above their pre-pandemic level in mid-August, though postings in areas like software development remain lower, underscoring how uneven conditions can be for people hunting for a job. Idekoba said Indeed data show that only 4% of US job changers, with at least a high-school degree, switched jobs last year with the help of a recruiter contacting them. The other 96%, he said, are left to apply on their own, often dozens of times, without receiving any responses. The frustrating silence some job seekers experience comes as recruiters are often sorting through more applications, with fewer colleagues to help. Greenhouse, which makes applicant-tracking software, analyzed some 640 million applications from more than 6,000 companies between 2022 and 2025. It found that applications per job more than doubled over that period, while the average number of recruiters per organization fell 56%. Jalonni Weaver, an in-house recruiter at a life insurance firm near Dallas, said that in her prior roles, spikes in applicants meant there wasn't always time to review each résumé. Such buildups, she said, can push employers to use technology to automatically screen candidates. That can turn the early stage of hiring into an AI-to-AI loop, Weaver said, as job seekers use chatbots to polish résumés and sometimes submit applications, while employers rely on the technology to sort applicants. Those systems often only look for a narrow set of keywords and can miss transferable experience, she said. "We're not hiring for perfection," Weaver said. "We're hiring for that real human, and we're hiring for your experience." The flood of automated applications has also put a premium on verification, Idekoba said. Indeed said it verifies employers before new job postings appear, a process that can include checking a work email associated with an employer and using a third-party identity check. The company also limits how long employers can post roles for free, which can require them to take an additional step to keep a listing live. For job seekers, Indeed uses phone verification among other measures to confirm a person's identity. It is also testing with select employers a feature that lets candidates show employers independently verified professional licenses. Verification can help establish who is applying, though Idekoba said some employers also need to change how they evaluate job seekers. Whirlpool's dividend suspension came with a 49% stock plunge, and four other high-yielding names are flashing the same warning signs that trapped income investors before the ax fell.  Income investors who chase the biggest yield often end up owning the biggest cut. Whirlpool has already shown how fast the trap can spring: management “made the prudent decision to suspend the common dividend to maximize our cash preservation, improving near-term liquidity” during a year in which the stock has fallen 49.15% year to date. Every name below carries at least one of the same warning signs. A dividend becomes unsustainable when the payout consistently outruns the earnings base a company actually generates (EPS for ordinary corporates), when free cash flow after capital spending will not cover it, or when the payout is being held together with borrowing while revenue and margins shrink. Whirlpool (NYSE:WHR | WHR Price Prediction) is the cautionary tale that sets the tone for this list. The appliance maker had been paying a quarterly dividend before the board suspended it, and the shares have been decimated: down 60.9% over the past year and 78.62% over five years, taking the market cap to roughly $2.30 billion. The math from recent earnings was brutal. Ongoing EPS came in at -$0.56 in Q1 2026 and -$0.21 in Q2, and free cash flow was “a consumption of approximately $1.1 billion” in the second quarter alone. Net debt sat at $5.8 billion, and interest expense for the year is guided near $350 million. Full-year free cash flow guidance of $300 million would not have supported the prior payout. Even if Whirlpool eventually restores a dividend, covenants on the $2.00 billion of secured bonds and asset-based facility will constrain how much cash can leave the company. Kraft Heinz (NASDAQ:KHC) has held its quarterly dividend at $0.40 per share in every recorded quarter from 2020 through the latest 2026 declaration. That looks stable until you compare it to the $0.625 paid in 2018: a payout that has stayed flat for years signals a “held” dividend under stress. Q2 FY26 delivered $7.4 billion in non-cash goodwill and intangible impairments, a direct signal of brand-value erosion, and produced a GAAP net loss of $5.46 billion on revenue of $6.26 billion. Full-year adjusted EPS is guided at $2.03 to $2.09 against an annualized dividend rate of $1.60, with interest expense of roughly $890 million and organic sales guided -0.5% to -2.0%. The bull case is that management is “preserving a very strong balance sheet and cash flow” while stepping up marketing. That still leaves adjusted EPS coverage of the payout tight if the brand investment does not restore volume. Conagra Brands (NYSE:CAG) is the second name on this list where the trap has already snapped. The quarterly dividend was reduced from $0.35 to $0.175 per share, an annualized rate of $0.70, with the first reduced payment made on September 2, 2026. Even at the lower rate, the recent earnings picture is not comfortable. FY27 adjusted EPS is guided at $1.40 to $1.50, net debt stands at $7.05 billion at 3.83x adjusted EBITDA, and organic net sales are guided -1% to -3%. FY26 saw $2.9 billion of impairments, and Q1 FY27 produced a GAAP net loss of $1.62 billion. The shares have fallen 19.06% over the past year. For the reset payout to hold, management needs the pricing, productivity, and volume recovery detailed on the call to actually stick. Dow (NYSE:DOW) trimmed its quarterly dividend from $0.70 to $0.35 beginning with the ex-dividend date of August 29, 2025. Shares have rebounded, up 28.34% year to date, but the five-year return remains -36.93%. Q1 2026 delivered a GAAP net loss of $445 million, before a Q2 rebound to $802 million in net income on a 30% surge in polyethylene prices. Management has made the priorities plain: “With improved earnings and cash conversion, we will prioritize any excess cash towards the deleveraging”, with Q3 EBITDA guided down to approximately $1.7 billion. Annual 2025 operating cash flow of $1.03 billion was well short of capital expenditures of $2.48 billion. The reset payout is safer than the old one, but a cyclical chemicals business with an investment-grade commitment and a heavy capex plan leaves less room than a 4%-plus headline yield suggests. T. Rowe Price (NASDAQ:TROW) is the softest warning on this list. The regular quarterly dividend has stepped up to $1.30, and adjusted diluted EPS of $2.57 in Q2 FY26 covers it comfortably. The balance sheet carries no debt burden. The problem in the case of T. Rowe Price is its direction. The firm ended Q2 with $1.9 trillion in assets under management and $6.5 billion in Q2 net outflows, after $13.70 billion of outflows in Q1. The effective fee rate has slipped to 38.1 basis points, and management said “Fundamental active equity remains under pressure, and we expect that to continue in the second half of the year”, with second-half flows likely “meaningfully more challenging than the first half.” The near-term payout looks safe. The real exposure is a market drawdown that would compress AUM, fees, and earnings all at once, precisely when a retiree needs stability most. Dividend cuts usually take the share price with them, which is exactly what happened at Whirlpool, Conagra, and Dow. Yield alone is never a buy thesis, and a payout that has been “held” through obvious operating stress is a warning worth heeding (we cataloged the seven signs a big yield is about to be cut in a free dividend trap guide). The right questions are always the same: does EPS cover the payout, does free cash flow cover it after capex, and is leverage rising to fund it? Login  Ivan  12 September 2026   Apple iOS Featured Hot take  Now that we've had a few days to mull over Apple's newest iPhones, it's time to share our initial thoughts. Some things are as clear as day - Apple will still sell every new iPhone that it manufactures, and it's almost a 100% certainty that it will struggle to keep the iPhone Duo in stock. With that out of the way, here's our hot take. Apple is said to have been actively working on its first foldable since at least 2019. Reportedly, Tim Cook came back from a trip to China, apparently very energized about foldables. We heard Apple would launch its first folding phone in 2023, then 2024, then we were almost sure it was going to happen in 2025. But it finally happened in 2026. And it's clear that Apple made smart use of all that time. In typical Apple fashion, the company arrived late to a significant product, but made it more refined than everyone else. And it made it its own way. The iPhone Duo looks to be a finished device, with a nearly crease-less inner display, solid and uncompromised build quality - it's one of a very select few dust-proof folding phones. The inner display has an anti-reflective coating, similar to the Honor Magic V6 and Galaxy Z Fold8's, a hardware trait we usually see on a product's sixth generation, not its first. But where the extra refinement and polish is most obvious is the iPhone Duo's software. The transition animation when opening and closing the Duo is reason enough for some people to buy the phone. The left-aligned dock is also a unique usability adjustment that could make using this phone nicer than any other foldable. Apple also said that Apple Pencil support is on its way, which is impressive! The iPhone Duo is made for right-handed people. Early hands-on impressions suggest that the dock can't be moved over to the left (yet, hopefully). Apple placed the volume button on the top of the Duo, and the jury's still out on whether that's a successful move or a dealbreaker. The $2,000 Duo's main camera looks to be the same one from the $700 iPhone 17e - an inferior 1/2.55-inch imager with a narrower 26mm lens, not the 48MP 1/1.28-inch unit from the Pro models. Apple went with an in-display camera on the inner display. These cameras are seriously inferior to a simple punch-hole alternative. We're also not sure if the name Duo has a good ring to it. Also, as a certain YouTuber said, it's 2026 and Apple has a device named Duo and one named Neo. The A20 Pro SoC is impressive. It's the world's first 2nm chip and is all about on-device AI. The processor is up to 20% faster, the graphics processor is 40% faster and has 1 more core, but the Neural Engine (the one that handles AI) has doubled the cores compared to the A19 Pro - 32 cores over 16 cores. The A20 Pro also reportedly increases memory bandwidth by 50%. This isn't a mere yearly spec bump; it's a major generational leap forward. The batteries on both Pro models are also increased, and so is runtime - the iPhone 18 Pro Max increases video playback by 6 hours over its predecessor, while the 18 Pro adds 3 hours. However, both phones get the same, slow, by 2026 standards, charging. The camera system is more or less unchanged. There will be some people who will be convinced that the new four-step variable aperture lens on the Pro models is a game-changer, but it really isn't, not on a phone anyway. We've had dozens such lens-equipped phones in the office, and we can't say it brings a worthwhile improvement to image quality. Technically speaking, closing the aperture to increase depth of field can be useful. But a tiny phone sensor and lens combination already has a huge depth of field in almost any scenario that isn't close to the minimum focusing distance (aka macro). So, in practice, shooting anything beyond 1 meter with a 24mm-equivalent lens on a 1/1.28-inch sensor at f/1.4 or f/4 won't produce a dramatic difference in depth of field. That's especially true for a landscape shot, where most of the scene will already be in focus. I can smell the comments section already! We have a few of those at the office, and nobody is jumping out of their seat to pre-order an 18 Pro model. There simply isn't enough to warrant buying the newer model over its predecessor, unless you really, really like Burgundy. Apple increased the prices of its 18 Pro models by $100 in the US, but it increased them by €150 and £100 in Europe. But there's more to the story - the base iPhone 18 Pro Max ($1,300, or an equivalent €1,120) in the US costs less than the base iPhone 18 Pro (€1,450) in Germany. Non-US buyers seemingly get the memory price hike tax to cover Apple's US market price difference. In China, prices are up by CNY 1,000. In India, they're up by INR 30,000. And in Japan, prices are hiked up by JPY 40,000. Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs. This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon. Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.  They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything". Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post. "We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X. While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm. Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products. Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species". One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic". He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology. "It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said. "Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'" Anthropic was valued at $965bn (Â£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year. The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements. In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious". They said he dismissed them as untrue. Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".   And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers. Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a duopoly in the sector. Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole". On Friday, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety. "Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective." Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's  proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety.  Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei. In April, Anthropic roiled the AI world when it said it found that its Mythos tool could outperform humans at some hacking and cybersecurity tasks. Mythos also showed the ability to independently escape what is known as the sandbox environment, setting off a debate among regulators, legislators and businesses about AI's potential dangers. In a new development on Thursday, Anthropic said it had found and stopped threat actors who were trying to use its AI technology for activity including the development of bioweapons and cyber-espionage.  Beneath the sparkling chandeliers hanging in the stained-glass dome atrium of The Palace Hotel, some investors told the BBC that the comments from Coxon and others could accelerate a government crackdown. Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now." But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal. David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic.  OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership". OpenAI, which announced in June that it would go public on the stock market, was most recently valued at $852bn. The company did not respond to a BBC inquiry seeking comment. At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI. One investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares. His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable? It has been edited for length and clarity.People often assume that I quit my six-figure job in product design because of severe burnout or an existential crisis, but that wasn't the case. I moved from Korea to Toronto in 2020 as an in-house product designer for a tech company, often creating mobile apps and websites. The paycheck was great — I was making about $173,000 to do a job that allowed me to have a fairly healthy work-life balance. I wasn't working 80 hours per week. Most weeks, I clocked about 40 hours, working mostly 9 to 5. Since my income was more than enough to live on, I was also able to travel when I had time off, never needing to worry about money or budgets. While I wouldn't say I loved the work, I liked it. The job was about making logical decisions, and then convincing stakeholders of my decisions through storytelling. It was my dream job as an immigrant, and it was sustainable. I could have carried on working it, but I had also been doing content creation on the side and had just signed a book deal. There weren't enough hours in the day to do all three. It would have been like having three full-time jobs. Debating which one to let go of, I decided to quit the most stable of the three — product design. Writing a book was very important to me, and I knew content creation would support the promotion of the book. But I was hesitant to abandon my only employed source of work. The thought was really scary. I remember having so much anxiety in the weeks leading up to my resignation in June 2026. Was it a mistake to leave a consistent paycheck in the middle of economic uncertainty? Would I be able to re-enter the market should I change my mind? I made a deal with myself to try and quell the anxiety that this was a permanent decision. For one year, I'd work for myself — pursuing content creation and book writing — and then I'd decide if I wanted to go back to the corporate world. The White House made a bunch of parody video games. We have more suggestions.  This week, the White House removed a Tetris-inspired game called Build the Wall from its recently launched arcade website after the Tetris Company publicly warned that it takes copyright law “very seriously.”  Here are a few options the White House might consider to replace the game: Players direct a round creature with a constantly moving mouth through a maze as he munches on tiny coins. Meanwhile, the ghosts of financial lawsuits past pursue Super PAC-Man—but consuming excerpts from favorable Supreme Court rulings allows him to temporarily devour these ghosts, too. Once Super PAC-Man collects all the coins, he progresses, unsatiated, to the next level, where he sends out a single text and all the money starts flowing directly toward him.  Players form new, hateful attacks in this Scrabble-like multiplayer game using letters cut from public-school textbooks, removed museum displays, and maps depicting the former Lake Ontario. Highest-scoring insults include: SCUZZY, ZANY, and LOW-IQ JOKER. Extra points are awarded for letters placed on various Random Capitalization Squares.  Up to four players race golf carts around a cartoonishly decorated beach club, crashing through boxes of classified documents to unlock power-ups including nuclear footballs and black markers for unlimited redactions. Between races, players can refuel at the gas pump, assuming they have collected the requisite 175,000 coins per gallon. The winner receives a golf trophy; second, third, and fourth place—as well as any observers or people simply standing nearby—get access to state secrets.  This game is all in the timing: Players must market their own cryptocurrency, then wait until just the right moment to cash out, crashing the currency and tanking other players’ life savings.  Modern-day pioneers move into a covered wagon after an eminent-domain order for the construction of a data center displaces them from their hometown. Drinking water is scarce, noise pollution is earsplitting, and morale is low as players try to survive the perilous journey to one of the few remaining corners of protected parkland. Inevitably, all players die when artificial general intelligence bioengineers a new form of dysentery.  In this first-person interior-design game, players gild every nook, cranny, and free patch of wall space in their virtual home office.  No longer beholden to child-labor regulations, players ages 6 to 8 design their own pickaxes before descending 1,500 feet down a shaft to mine bituminous coal. Open-world play means that the only limit is kids’ imagination and black lung and tunnel collapse.  Players battle conservationists, historians, and patrons of the arts atop a revered memorial building, destroying it in the process. Downloadable content expands play to the Reflecting Pool, the National Mall, and the East Wing of the White House.  Players rearrange foods that were once safe to eat into matching groups to make them disappear as part of an FDA recall. But miss just one, and players will contract a parasitic infection that sends them to the hospital, where they will incur astronomical medical bills, which will prevent them from qualifying for a mortgage, which will force them to move back in with their parents.  A zombie occupies the most powerful office in the world. At the conclusion of Level 2, President Evil might insist that the game isn’t over, but so long as it works as intended, someone else will finally get a turn to play. It's the latest wearable tech boom that is likely coming to a street, park or town square near you. But not everyone sees the future of smart glasses as rose-tinted. The technology allows users to make calls, interact with AI hands-free and also take photos and videos simply by touching the frames, provoking concerns about privacy. Wetherspoons, which runs almost 800 pubs across the UK, has banned using the glasses to film inside its premises and women's rights campaigners have raised issues about their potential use for harassment. But, with videos from content creators continuing to thrive on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram, the debate of how to best use the glasses in public places will continue to go back and forth. Pearse Vallely is one of those content creators – the 31-year-old from Ballymurphy, in west Belfast, makes a living from his work on social media. He uses a pair of Meta Ray-Ban glasses, with most of his videos showing his glasses-eye view of walking down the street as he greets passers-by with rhyming phrases. One of his most popular videos, filmed in Belfast city centre, hit 600,000 views on TikTok. The success of the videos rely on their good-natured vibe. He said he had never posted a video after being asked not to, and no one had ever got in touch to ask him to take down a video. "I think it's because of the nature of my conversation with them. They know I'm not making an eejit out of them, I'm doing it in a positive way." Meta glasses, the brand used by Vallely, are the market leader in the smart glasses boom, with the company saying more than seven million pairs have been sold to date. Available for a few hundred pounds, and made in partnership with the firm behind famed sunglasses brand Ray-Bans, the frames feature an unobtrusive camera that users can activate via touch. This turns on a pulsing white light, which aims to let people know when a video is being taken, and a flash for photos – a feature a Meta spokesperson said "smartphones and other cameras don't have". Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered with. Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years. Valelly, whose videos rely on the interactions being spontaneous and natural, said people are often aware he is recording due to the light on his glasses. He also said he tries to let people know he has recorded them after filming if he can catch them in time. In Northern Ireland, it is generally legal to film someone even discreetly in a public place, as people in public do not usually have a reasonable expectation of privacy. The filming would only be unlawful if it could be seen as harassment, stalking, if the footage is voyeuristic, or in circumstances where there would be a reasonable expectation of privacy. "It's okay to have a 30-second conversation with someone," Vallely said. "I think that's something we're losing due to technology, and I'm trying to use technology to spin it around." Vallely said he could understand the reasoning behind banning wearing Meta glasses "if people are being crude and rude", but he said the intention behind filming was key. "People know it's me doing it, while other people do it on troll accounts. No matter what is invented, people are going to use things for the wrong reasons." Still, while Vallely said he hasn't run into any opposition, there are reports suggesting an increased friction between people using the glasses to film and the general public. Last December, people hailed a woman as "a hero" after she snapped a man's Meta glasses in two on the New York subway.  In July, police in Scotland began an investigation after complaints over a TikToker who used the glasses to secret film members of the public. Referring to the company's ban on filming, a Wetherspoons spokesperson said smart glasses breached "common sense by enabling surreptitious surveillance" while Monopoly Events, which runs Comic Con Northern Ireland, also banned wearing the glasses at its events over concerns about secret recording. Meanwhile, TikTok videos of users approaching women, asking for their number and filming their reaction to pick-up lines, are often posted with the hashtag #howtogetagirlfriend and can garner thousands of views. Elaine Crory, a women's sector lobbyist at the Women's Resource and Development Agency, said there's a lack of awareness about when and how the glasses are being used, leading to issues around consent. "Right now, if you're filming with a camera or with your phone, I usually can see that and then avoid that. But you may not be aware you're being filmed with an AI camera." She added there were also concerns the glasses were being used for things that are currently illegal, like upskirting. Crory said people can appeal to social media sites to take videos down and some venues have put up signs "on a case by case basis", but she feels legislation has not caught up with the technology. "A person has no legal redress if they are filmed in the street, on a bus, in a classroom," she said. The Department of Justice (DoJ) said that while the regulation of Meta glasses was not a DoJ specific matter, if the use of the glasses involved "behaviour that crosses the criminal threshold, then existing offences such as 'up-skirting' as a form of voyeurism" were available. For optometrist Geoff McConville, who stocks Meta glasses in his Belfast shop, there are concerns about their "inappropriate use", but there are also beneficial aspects to the technology. He cites how his patients use text-to-speech features, allowing them to read newspapers and signs with AI. "For my elderly, visually impaired patients, they are ground-breaking. They are amazing." In a statement, Meta said the glasses provided "critical new technology for people who are low-sighted or hard of hearing and limiting how people can use this technology would be a major step backwards". "Naturally some places shouldn't be filmed at all and that's reasonable but rules should be applied consistently." In a recent Q&A session, the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said if people posted content "taking advantage of people and harassing them... then we're going to take the content down".
